# Iran weaponized the Strait of Hormuz. Now its neighbors are building around it

![A vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on July 16.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/2026-07-16t062529z-1977252053-rc2qemaixj4i-rtrmadp-3-iran-crisis-oman-hormuz.JPG?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

*Brett McGurk is a CNN global affairs analyst who served in senior national security positions under Presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden.*

Wars often end somewhere different from where they begin.

The current conflict with Iran has been plagued by ill-defined and shifting objectives, from aspirations of regime change to more focused aims of degrading Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities.

Nearly six months in, it has evolved into something else entirely: a struggle over who controls the Strait of Hormuz and, with it, one of the world’s most important arteries for global energy. Iran has demonstrated both the capability and willingness to target commercial shipping passing through the strait unless conducted under rules Tehran prescribes.

The US – and much of the world, including all the Gulf states adjacent to the strait – has rightly deemed that unacceptable.

The strategic objective now is increasingly about one issue. Does the Strait of Hormuz remain an international waterway, or does Iran acquire the ability to determine who passes through it and under what conditions? Ceding control to Iran
events.summary: CNN values your feedback Iran weaponized the Strait of Hormuz.

# GRAINS-Grains market reaches new highs after Black Sea attacks and crude oil rally

Posted to [Maritime Reporter](/blogs/blogs-maritime_reporter)
on
July 24, 2026

Wheat prices have surged to their highest level in two years due to the escalating attacks on Black Sea ports and shipping. This has sparked new concerns about food inflation, as one of world's major grain export routes is under threat.

Corn prices have also risen to their highest level in over a year. Traders warn that disruptions in grain flow from the Black Sea may increase food costs for producers and consumers around the world.

Black Sea grain exports are a major part of the global grain trade, with cargoes coming from Russia, Ukraine and other major grain producers. However, recent threats against vessels and ports have raised fears that the Black Sea could become a difficult route for exporters to get their crops to Africa, the Middle East, and Asia.

Commerzbank stated in a report that disruptions in the area have a direct effect on wheat prices.

The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT), the most active wheat market, was up 1.1% to $7.03-3/4 per bushel at 1021 GMT. It had earlier reached a 2-year high of $7.11-1/4. This puts it on course for a gain of more than 20% this month.

Chicago wheat prices rose on Friday as the market was poised to post a fourth weekly gain. Prices were also trading near a two-year high. This was due to attacks on grain ships and port infrastructures in the Black Sea Region.

Corn hovered around a 15-month high on the backs of a rally in crude prices. Soybeans also gained ground, trading at their highest level since May 2024.

One grains trader from Singapore said that the focus on the?wheat markets is tightening supply, given what's happening in Russia and Ukraine. This is the peak season for exports in the Black Sea Region and if this continues, buyers will be looking for alternative cargoes.

As of?0221 GMT, the most active wheat contract on Chicago Board of Trade was up 0.3% to $6.98-1/2 per bushel.

Soybeans rose 0.2% to $12.45-3/4 per bushel. This is not far off their previous session high of?May 2024. Corn increased by 0.2% to $4.88-1/4 a bushel after reaching its highest level since April of last year.

The attacks on grain handling infrastructure and ships in Russia and Ukraine have raised concerns about global supplies.

# No War for Old Men

The fall of Ukraine’s top general, Oleksandr Syrsky, leaves younger officers to finish the reforms that he resisted.

By [Simon Shuster](https://www.theatlantic.com/author/simon-shuster/)

Angela Weiss / AFP / Getty

Drone warfare took a while to catch on in Ukraine. Like any revolution, it required a struggle. The opposition came mostly from the older generals trained to fight using artillery and tanks. Early in the war with Russia, many of them saw drones as toys, better suited to taking aerial photos of wedding parties than flying missions over the battlefield. But a coalition of junior officers and tech enthusiasts saw early on that drones could hold the key to Ukraine’s defense, even its victory.

The course of the war has proved the younger generation right. Drones now account for more than 80 percent of all battlefield casualties. They have made tanks and artillery look like lumbering relics in the war zone. Through long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure, drones have also forced Moscow to play defense. But it took years for the technology to gain broad acceptance.

# China Protests Trump’s Latest Tariffs

Published

Jul 24, 2026 at 07:32 AM EDT

updated

Jul 24, 2026 at 09:48 AM EDT

![Micah McCartney](https://assets.newsweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/2445735-micah.jpg?w=1600&quality=80&webp=1)

Reporter

Beijing has protested President Donald Trump's new tariffs on China and 59 other countries.

The duties [target governments](https://www.newsweek.com/new-tariffs-donald-trump-countries-list-map-trade-12237599) deemed to have failed to sufficiently enforce or prohibit forced labor, which officials say gives foreign producers an unfair advantage by allowing goods to be made with below-market labor costs.

*Newsweek* reached out to the White House for comment outside regular office hours.

#### Read More on World

"We oppose all forms of unilateral tariffs," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said during the ministry's daily press briefing on Friday, warning: "Tariff wars and trade wars do not serve any party's interests."

[China](/topic/china)—one of the United States' largest trading partners—and Hong Kong were among the countries placed in the 12.5 percent tariff bracket under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, up from the temporary 10 percent rate that expired Friday.

Imports from Japan, South Korea and Vietnam—the U.S.' fifth, sixth, and ninth largest trading partners, respectively—are also subject to the 12.5 percent rate.
